extracted.intended_audience: general readers; online community members and moderators; researchers and journalists interested in internet culture and online harassment
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize criteria, behaviors, types, motivations, effects, and mitigations of online trolling for readers, moderators, and researchers. Covers definitions, psychological correlates, legal aspects, message designs, and response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: In slang, trolling is when a person posts deliberately offensive or provocative messages online (such as in social media, a forum, a chat room, an online video game) or performs similar behaviors in real life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These messages can be inflammatory, insincere, digressive, extraneous, or off-topic, and may have the intent of provoking others into displaying emotional responses or manipulating others' perceptions. The behavior is typically for the troll's amusement or to achieve a specific result such as disrupting a rival's online activities or purposefully causing confusion or harm to other people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods / behavioral characteristics of trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling behaviors involve tactical aggression to incite emotional responses and may include posting inflammatory, insincere, off-topic, or misleading content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include posting insults, off-topic bait, misleading re-posts, deliberate provocation. Tactics can range from benign humor to sadistic harassment; they may disseminate bad advice or damage trust in an online community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent and motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling may be motivated by amusement (lulz), a desire for attention, power derived from upsetting others, identity play, political manipulation, or to achieve disruption or confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivations range from 'gentle inside joke' community bonding to organized state/corporate manipulation. Understanding intent helps distinguish provocative-but-legitimate contributions from malicious trolling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response strategy: 'Don't feed the trolls' (ignore)
rubrics_metrics.description: One common strategy for dealing with online trolls is to ignore them; 'don't feed the trolls' is based on the idea that trolls feed on attention and reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychologists consider withholding attention the best way to stop trolling, though an extinction burst (a temporary increase in disruptive behavior after ignoring) can occur. Advice often recommended for moderators and users: avoid engagement, apply moderation tools, remove provocative content where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grades/types of trolling (NetLingo classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: NetLingo suggests four grades of trolling: playtime trolling, tactical trolling, strategic trolling, and domination trolling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grades reflect increasing sophistication and harmful intent: from light-hearted insider jokes to organized campaigns aiming to dominate or severely disrupt discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and identity deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Anonymity and identity deception facilitate trolling: trolls often hide behind anonymous accounts or fake usernames and sometimes deliberately impersonate legitimate participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity deception can be used to pass as a bona fide group member (trolling as a game of identity deception), or produce sockpuppet armies. Moderation can address this by verification, stronger identity cues, and detection of multiple accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological characteristics correlated with trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Research correlates trolling with personality traits such as sadism, psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and the dark triad/tetrad; trolling behavior qualifies as antisocial and is associated with deriving pleasure from others' suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report men are more likely to troll, and anonymity increases incidence. This informs expectations about motives and possible interventions (e.g., accountability measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concern trolling
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern trolls pretend to be sympathetic to a position while covertly criticizing it; they declare interest in joining a cause but subtly ridicule or sow doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concern trolling aims to sow fear, uncertainty, and doubt within groups by feigning concern (example: fake 'concern' for public health used to shame a group). Detection requires attention to rhetorical patterns and consistency of position.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-sponsored / corporate / special-interest trolling and 'Wikipedia troll' message design
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations and governments may employ trolls (sockpuppet armies, astroturfing) to manipulate public opinion. The NATO report describes a 'Wikipedia troll' who reposts essentially true information without emotional value but in the wrong context to mislead readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such actors often use coordinated, large-scale campaigns; detection requires media-literacy, critical thinking, and analysis of coordination patterns. Examples include China's '50 Cent Party' and documented state-directed campaigns in hybrid warfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environments that foster trolling (troll sites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain online spaces (anonymous message boards like 4chan or TOTSE) are recognized as hotspots for trolling because anonymity and culture enable provocative behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places with limited traceability and cultures that reward shock or disruption are fertile ground for trolls. Moderation policy, community norms, and registration requirements influence prevalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early/benign forms of trolling (insider humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Usenet-style trolling could be a gentle inside joke used to identify newcomers and serve as a positive group-defining practice (e.g., 'trolling for newbies').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between community-internal playful trolling and external destructive trolling; context and community norms determine whether a behavior is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on targets and communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling can upset or harm targets, disseminate misinformation, damage trust in online communities, lead to harassment and real-world consequences, and can quickly brand new users as trolls in sensitized groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include emotional harm, reputational damage, loss of participation, and spread of confusion or false narratives. Moderators should consider both individual welfare and community health when responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal frameworks and criminal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal treatment of trolling varies: cyberbullying laws differ by jurisdiction; trolling is not a single federal crime in the U.S.; other countries have specific laws (e.g., UK Malicious Communications Act 1988 and Communications Act 2003, Japan's ban on online insults).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where laws apply, penalties can include fines and imprisonment (examples cited include up to two years in the UK). Moderators and users should be aware of local legal standards when escalating incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation strategies and platform measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms and communities use measures such as requiring commenter registration, moderation, bans, content removal, and using human review combined with technology to identify platform manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Reuters, Facebook, and others requiring names/emails to increase accountability; Twitter uses technology + human review to identify platform manipulation; transparency and archives for state-backed operations help public awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling as subculture and ritual behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling has become its own subculture with rituals, rules, specialized language, and dedicated spaces, driven by the pursuit of 'lulz' and the performative role of the trickster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding subcultural norms (e.g., celebration of anonymity, in-group humour) helps contextualize behaviours and inform moderation/community response strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated detection and research
rubrics_metrics.description: Research efforts focus on automated detection of bots, cyborgs, and trolling behavior and on causes of trolling (e.g., 'Anyone Can Become a Troll').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies explore behavioral markers, coordination signals, and personality correlates; practical application includes bot detection, anomaly detection, and classifier development combined with human oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trolling tactics and personas (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common tactics/personas include playing a 'well-meaning moron' (Ken M) who escalates absurdity until exposed, hoaxes (Gold Membership scams), posting true information out-of-context, and impersonation/fake accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizing recurring tactic patterns (feigned ignorance, escalating absurdity, bait-and-switch, context-shift) aids identification and response. Historical examples illustrate how these tactics fool newcomers and media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misapplication and subjectivity of the label 'troll'
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the term 'troll' is subjective; some may characterize a post as trolling while others see it as a legitimate (even controversial) contribution. The word is sometimes incorrectly used to refer to anyone with controversial opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-broad labeling; consider intent, pattern, and context before classifying someone as a troll to prevent unjust exclusion or mismoderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group dynamics and psychological mechanisms (flaming vs trolling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trolling and flaming overlap but have distinctions; mechanisms such as deindividuation and disinhibition (enhanced by anonymity) help explain why people engage in trolling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the difference (flaming as direct anger vs trolling as provocation/identity play) and the underlying psychology can shape interventions focused on identity cues, community norms, and accountability.
